Comments for authors:
The authors propose a system for training large language models on hardware connected over the public internet and distributed around the world. This is a difficult problem (EleutherAI writes that “doing volunteer-driven distributed compute well for this use case is an unsolved problem”) and the authors tackle it with a combination of pipelining and data parallelism.

As this setting can’t assume homogeneous network performance, the parallelism assignment problem is much more difficult than it is in datacenters, and the authors apply a novel combination of algorithmic approaches to solve it, including treating pipelining and data parallelism independently and scheduling parallel units onto workers using an evolutionary algorithm.

The authors report benchmark results on a series of increasingly heterogeneous network configurations, showing significant speedup relative to a grid-search-optimized Megatron setup with homogeneous data and pipeline parallelism.


The authors do a good job of motivating the problem and pointing out weaknesses in existing systems (e.g. a focus on data parallelism or mixture-of-experts models).

The paper uses the terminology “macro-batch” but it’s sometimes unclear whether this refers to the portion of the global batch that runs on one data-parallel replica, or to the portion that runs on one stage of one data-parallel replica (more often called a microbatch). I’d recommend being a little clearer here.

The algorithm the authors introduce seems reasonable and well-motivated. If it’s fast enough, and if decomposing the assignment problem into separate data and pipeline levels isn’t a restrictive assumption (both of these appear to be true!) then it also seems like the only algorithm we need for this problem. (It might be possible to optimize in an even greedier way, but if the evolutionary approach is fast enough I’m not sure it matters).

I’m somewhat disappointed that a system for heterogeneous distributed training (justified in part by a seemingly accurate claim that home electricity is 50-100x cheaper than spot GPU instances) was benchmarked only on cloud machines with cloud networking, not on machines with conventional home internet. But it looks like the bandwidth between distant datacenters in the authors’ experiments is low enough that it might be representative of home network connections.

The authors present good benchmarks against grid-search-optimized Megatron configurations, and their ablations, although brief, are convincing about the value of their local search strategy.


How much do you lose by decomposing the assignment problem into separate data and pipeline levels? I think the answer might be “nothing”, but it would be great to be more explicit about that.

The intra-node bandwidth is quoted as 100 Gb/s in your experiments, but IIUC V100 NVlink is 150 GB/s (1200 Gb/s); is there a reason this isn’t the right number to use for intra-node bandwidth? And in general, are the bandwidths you’re assuming the result of benchmarks? If so, maybe include those benchmarks somewhere?

Were the benchmarks run on cloud machines that were really physically located in different regions, or were the bandwidths between machines limited artificially to simulate inter-region connections?


The authors are clear about most of the limitations of their system, including lack of online failure handling and dynamic replanning.

Summary:
This paper proposed a few-shot learning approach for interactive segmentation. Given a set of user-annotated points, the proposed model learns to generate dense segmentation masks of objects. To incorporate the point-wise annotation, the guidance network is introduced. The proposed idea is applied to guided image segmentation, semantic segmentation, and video segmentation.

Clarity:
Overall, the presentation of the paper can be significantly improved. First of all, it is not clear what the problem setting of this paper is, as it seems to have two sets of training data of fully-annotated images (for training) and the combined set of point-wise annotated images and unannotated images (guidance images T in the first equation); It is not clear whether authors generate the second dataset out of the first one, or they have separate datasets for these two. Also, it is not clear how the authors incorporate the unannotated images for training. 

The descriptions on model architecture are also not quite clear, as it involves two components (g and f) but start discussing with g without providing a clear overview of the combined model (I would suggest changing the order of Section 4.1 and Section 4.2 to make it clearer). The loss functions are introduced in the last part of the method, which makes it also very difficult to understand. 

Originality and significance:
The technical contribution of the paper is very limited. I do not see many novel contributions in terms of both network architecture and learning perspective.

Experiment:
Overall, I am not quite convinced with the experiment results. The method is compared against only a few (not popular) interactive segmentation methods, although there exist many recent works addressing the same task (e.g. Xu et al. 2016). 

The experiment settings are also not clearly presented. For instance, what is the dataset used for the evaluation of the first paragraph in section 5.1? How do you split the Pascal VOC data to exclusive sets? How do you sample point-wise annotation from dense mask labels? How does the sampling procedure affect the performance? 

The performance of the guided semantic segmentation is also quite low, limiting the practical usefulness of the method. Finally, the paper does not present qualitative results, which are essential to understanding the performance of the segmentation system. 

Minor comments:
1. There are a lot of grammar issues. Please revise your draft.
2. Please revise the notations in equations. For instance, 
    T = {{(x_1, L_1),...} \cup {\bar{x}_1,...}
    L_s = {(p_j,l_j):j\in{1,...,P}, l\in{1,...,K}\cup{\emptyset}}
    Also, in the next equation, j\in\bar{x}_q} -> p_ j\in\bar{x}_q} (j is an index of pixel)

The paper presents a multipass streaming algorithm for rank-r SVD.  Given an input matrix X in R^{mxn} the algorithm identifies two matrices V* in R^{nxr} and H in R^{rxr}. V* has orthonormal columns that span the top r right singular vectors.  H rotates V* so that V*H = Vr, where Vr in R^{nxr} is the matrix of the top-r right singular vectors.  V* and H are computed by minibatch gradient descent, trained until convergence with custom loss functions.  V* is computed in the first stage and then H in the second stage. 

The algorithm is accurate and uses very little storage.

The main selling point of the algorithm is that the memory needed is only O(rn), as opposed to O(r(m+n)) for competing algorithms and the result is exact as opposed to approximate.  The way this reduction is achieved is by allowing multiple streaming passes over the rows of X, whereas the competing algorithms only allow 1 pass.  This would be useful when the dataset is so large that storing a copy of the data is prohibitive and that is a realistic setting in the modern data-science workflow.

Indeed, for the purpose of dimensionality reduction it might even be sensible to only to complete stage 1.  That's because many algorithms, e.g. linear/logistic regression, kernel methods with the Euclidean kernel, and many neural network architectures, will be agnostic to the rotation H.

One small theoretical disadvantage is that the number of passes required is not known.  The authors state at most 5 passes are necessary, but actually that number was determined empirically and your number of passes depends on the number of epochs to convergence in stage 1.

Table 1 states that Range-Net space complexity is r*(n+r), however Appendix E.3 states that the implementation dumps XV*, an intermediate mxr matrix, to disk.  Specificly E.3 states "The output data [of stage 1] is dumped onto the secondary memory assuming that storing a low rank approximation is still main memory intensive. For Stage 2, this low rank approximation in the secondary memory is streamed as input, and the extracted singular values and vectors are saved in main memory." so the authors' implementation actually requires r*(m+n) storage."

I think it is misleading that the implementation does not obey the claimed memory bound.  It is true that the algorithm can be implemented without dumping XV*, but it requires more compute and passes to recalculate XV* during stage 2 and still more to compute the actual singular values.  How this extra compute affect the time required for the approximation?

In terms of writing, I think that the paper is poorly organized.  The main drawback is that there is no clear and concise description of the algorithm.  Parts of the algorithm are described in Section 3 and Appendix E, but Section 3 also contains the statements of correctness interspersed with the description.  There are terms left undefined and dimensions of matrices are only identified haphazardly.

Other notes:
. Please formally define tail energy.
. Section 1.2.  "In the absence of ... different from SVD factors".  I didn't understand this sentence at all and Equation (1) does not include any decomposition.
. I found the description of the algorithm as a neural network confusing. The network is two layers that each consist of a single matrix multiplication,  it's two single matrix multiplications which are solved for independently.
. Figure 4 caption does not match the subfigure captions

This paper presents an interesting result, demonstrating the impossibility of provably efficient batch reinforcement learning (RL) under only two assumptions: a) Realizability and b) Feature Coverage. The authors provide persuasive counter-examples where the state/action space is polynomially dependent on the horizon $H$, yet the sample complexity exhibits an exponential dependence on $H$ with high probability.

However, I have some reservations regarding the Feature Coverage assumption. Unlike the Concentrability assumption [Chen & Jiang (2019), Xie & Jiang (2020a)], Feature Coverage merely postulates that the feature covariance matrix has a minimum eigenvalue of $1/d$. My specific concerns are as follows:
1. Is the Concentrability assumption mathematically more stringent than the Feature Coverage assumption? If so, why is Feature Coverage a primary focus when Chen & Jiang (2019) have already established the necessity of Concentrability for efficient batch RL?
2. Does the Feature Coverage assumption truly capture the notion of exploration within a batch dataset? From an RL perspective, exploration is critical both empirically and theoretically. In the constructed hard instance, crucial states $s_h^*$ are not even within the support of the dataset (which might also violate the Concentrability assumption). While I understand this is necessary to derive the exponential lower bound, it raises questions about the practical representativeness of Feature Coverage for exploratory datasets.
3. Theorem 5.1 is somewhat perplexing. While I grasp that its primary objective is to illustrate Error Amplification, why is an upper bound considered instead of a lower bound? Alternatively, is Section 5's aim to demonstrate that Error Amplification is unavoidable under the Realizability and Feature Coverage assumptions?

In conclusion, I find this paper to be well-written and it effectively addresses its central question under the specified assumptions. I have reviewed the proofs and found no significant errors. While I harbor some doubts about the practical reasonableness of certain assumptions in the context of RL, I maintain a positive outlook on this work. My concerns might be unfounded, and I eagerly anticipate further discussion.

The paper introduces P-DQN, a novel reinforcement learning algorithm designed to directly handle hybrid action spaces that combine discrete and continuous actions, without resorting to relaxation or discretization. By integrating mechanisms from DQN and DDPG, P-DQN extends the DQN framework to include a deterministic policy for continuous action parameters. The algorithm is evaluated in the context of training an AI agent for the popular mobile game *King of Glory* (KOG), where the hybrid action space arises naturally from in-game mechanics.

The core contributions are well-motivated, as hybrid action spaces are common in many real-world applications, such as robotics and game AI. The proposed method is conceptually simple and aligns intuitively with established RL frameworks. However, the empirical evaluation is insufficient in scope and depth. The experiments are limited to a single environment (KOG), which, while relevant, does not fully demonstrate the generality of the proposed approach. The authors should explore additional environments, such as modified versions of Atari games where action repetition or parameterized actions are explicitly modeled, as suggested in the work of Lakshminarayanan et al. (2017).

Comparisons are currently limited to DDPG, but broader baselines, such as PPO (Schulman et al., 2017), or variants that discretize the hybrid action space, would strengthen the analysis. Furthermore, the reward function is highly engineered, and the paper lacks an analysis of how individual components contribute to learning. A clearer understanding of the learned policy, convergence behavior, and the impact of hyperparameters (such as the two-timescale update rates α and β) is essential.

The paper also omits a discussion of the loss function formulation. While the current approach sums Q-values across discrete action indices, alternative formulations—such as using a product or weighted aggregation—may yield different trade-offs. Additionally, the use of non-Markovian reward components (e.g., changes in gold or hitpoints over time) could interfere with learning, particularly in settings where the Markov assumption is critical.

Finally, the paper suffers from grammatical and stylistic issues, which detract from its overall clarity and professionalism. Addressing these would improve its readiness for publication at a top-tier venue like ICLR.

Following Mancilla et al. (2017), this paper presents a theoretical investigation of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) in the stochastic convex optimization framework, focusing on the surprising failure of without-replacement SGD to achieve vanishing empirical risk and generalization gap, despite its classical convergence guarantees for population risk. The authors establish problem instances where one-pass without-replacement SGD attains Ω(1) empirical risk and generalization gap, challenging the stability and uniform convergence-based explanations for SGD’s generalization. They contrast this with with-replacement SGD, which achieves optimal population risk rates, and extend their analysis to multi-epoch regimes in finite-sum optimization. The work contributes to the understanding of algorithmic stability and generalization in non-ERM settings.

## Strengths
- **Originality**: The paper challenges conventional wisdom by demonstrating that without-replacement SGD can exhibit poor empirical risk minimization and generalization, even in convex settings. This contradicts the intuition that SGD implicitly regularizes solutions to achieve low generalization error, and it highlights limitations of existing generalization frameworks.
- **Technical Depth**: The construction of problem instances where SGD without replacement fails to generalize is theoretically non-trivial and rigorously executed. The separation between with- and without-replacement SGD variants is novel and insightful.
- **Significance**: The results have implications for the theoretical foundations of optimization and generalization, particularly in contexts where uniform convergence fails to explain algorithm behavior. The improved multi-epoch bounds for finite-sum problems are also practically relevant.

## Weaknesses
- **Practical Relevance**: While the constructed problem instances are valid theoretically, their prevalence in real-world scenarios (e.g., standard deep learning tasks) is unclear. The paper could better motivate whether such instances arise in practice or are primarily pathological.
- **Interpretation Gaps**: The analysis focuses on convex settings, but modern machine learning often involves non-convex objectives. The paper does not discuss whether similar phenomena occur in non-convex settings or how its results relate to SGD’s empirical success in deep learning.
- **Limited Discussion of Assumptions**: The reliance on one-pass SGD (without data reuse) and the specific problem construction (e.g., compact domain, convexity) could be further contextualized. For instance, how sensitive are the Ω(1) lower bounds to the choice of step size or domain diameter?

## Questions
1. The Ω(1) lower bounds rely on problem instances with specific loss structures. Are there natural conditions (e.g., strong convexity, Lipschitz gradients) under which without-replacement SGD avoids these pitfalls, even in one-pass settings?
2. The paper attributes the failure of without-replacement SGD to its lack of algorithmic stability. Does this imply that stability is a necessary condition for generalization in SCO, and if so, how does this reconcile with classical results where population risk converges despite non-vanishing generalization gaps?
3. How does the multi-epoch analysis for finite-sum problems reconcile with the single-epoch lower bounds? Does data permutation across epochs mitigate the issues observed in one-pass SGD?

## Suggestions
- Provide intuition or geometric illustrations for why without-replacement SGD fails in the constructed instances, to aid reader understanding.
- Discuss whether the observed phenomena depend on the dimension \(d\) or problem scaling (e.g., domain diameter, gradient norms).
- Explore connections to recent works on algorithmic stability in non-ERM settings, such as stochastic optimization with heavy-tailed noise or non-smooth objectives.
- Clarify the practical implications for hyperparameter choices (e.g., step size schedules, batch size) in finite-sum optimization when using multi-epoch without-replacement SGD.

Overall, this work makes a valuable theoretical contribution by exposing limitations of SGD’s generalization in specific convex settings, with implications for the analysis of optimization algorithms beyond uniform convergence. However, its relevance to non-convex optimization and real-world applications warrants further discussion.

This paper introduces HALP, a hardware-aware structural pruning method that frames latency-constrained model compression as a global optimization problem. The core idea revolves around combining latency reduction estimates (via lookup tables) with accuracy-aware saliency scores to determine optimal filter pruning strategies under target latency budgets. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in throughput across architectures like ResNet-50 and SSD while maintaining competitive accuracy, suggesting practical utility for deployment on edge devices.

The approach’s strength lies in its pragmatic focus on real hardware latency—a metric often overlooked in favor of proxy measures like FLOPs. The integration of saliency scores with latency-aware grouping feels intuitive, and the cross-task validation (classification + detection) adds credibility. However, the paper leaves several breadcrumbs unanswered: While the knapsack formulation is mentioned, the specifics of the "augmented" solver remain opaque. How does it differ from vanilla knapsack approaches used in prior work? Is the solver’s complexity manageable for very large networks, or does it become a bottleneck?

Another curiosity is the treatment of latency predictability. Lookup tables are standard practice, but hardware execution times can be non-linear (e.g., due to memory bottlenecks or parallelization). The paper assumes a linear relationship between pruned filters and latency reduction. Would this hold for architectures with heavy branching or heterogeneous operators? A brief discussion on such edge cases would strengthen the method’s generalizability claims.

The empirical results, while solid, could benefit from more granularity. For instance, the ResNet-50 pruning achieves +0.3% accuracy with 1.6× throughput—impressive, but how does this trade-off curve look at intermediate pruning ratios? Are there "sweet spots" where latency gains plateau while accuracy remains stable? Similarly, the SSD pruning’s 0.56 mAP drop for 1.94× speedup sounds reasonable, but context matters: is this drop concentrated in certain object classes or sizes? A breakdown could inform practitioners about task-specific suitability.

A minor gripe lies in the novelty framing. The global resource allocation perspective isn’t entirely new—prior works like AMC [1] similarly optimize for latency via reinforcement learning. HALP’s differentiation via saliency-weighted knapsack solving isn’t sufficiently contrasted against these alternatives. Is the main advantage computational efficiency during search, or does the formulation inherently capture better trade-offs? Clarifying this would help position the work within the pruning landscape.

Finally, the broader impact claim—"significantly impacting autonomous vehicles"—feels under-supported. While latency reduction is critical for real-time systems, the paper doesn’t validate HALP under dynamic inference scenarios (e.g., varying batch sizes or sensor inputs). Including such experiments, even preliminarily, would better bridge the gap between lab benchmarks and real-world deployment.

Suggestions: (1) Elaborate on the knapsack solver’s mechanics and complexity analysis; (2) Include ablation studies isolating the impact of latency-aware grouping vs. saliency scoring; (3) Discuss hardware-specific limitations (e.g., GPUs vs. NPUs); (4) Compare search time/efficiency against RL-based methods like AMC. Addressing these could elevate HALP from a strong empirical contribution to a more foundational advancement in hardware-aware pruning.

[1] Hu et al., "AMC: AutoML for Model Compression and Acceleration on Mobile Devices," ECCV 2018.

This paper introduces an interesting new way to tackle program synthesis, which is essentially about automatically creating code based on a set of instructions. The authors point out two main weaknesses in current AI-driven program synthesis methods: first, they often miss the fact that many different programs can produce the same result (what they call "aliasing"), and second, they don't really leverage the fact that programs have a very strict grammar that can be easily checked.

To fix the aliasing problem, the authors suggest using reinforcement learning. Instead of trying to generate one specific "correct" program, their method aims to create any program that works. They've come up with a new objective function that focuses on making sure the generated programs are semantically correct. This approach really seems to boost the system's ability to generalize, especially when there isn't a lot of training data available.

For the second issue, they've integrated a syntax checker that helps narrow down the possibilities when the system is trying to generate code. They also propose a clever way to learn both the syntax rules and the program synthesis model at the same time, which is super helpful if you don't already have a syntax checker. They show how well their ideas work using Karel, a beginner-friendly programming language often used in grid-based environments.

The paper itself is well-written and easy to follow, making their complex ideas quite clear. The experimental results are pretty impressive too, showing that their method consistently outperforms existing ones in terms of generalization. Both the use of reinforcement learning and the syntax checking component are genuinely fresh contributions to the field.

That said, there are a few areas where the paper could be stronger. It would be great to get more nitty-gritty details on how they implemented the syntax checker and that joint learning method. Also, more comparisons with other existing methods, particularly concerning how computationally efficient and scalable their approach is, would really strengthen the arguments. Finally, it would be exciting to see if their method can be applied to more complex programming languages and real-world scenarios.

Overall, this paper makes a significant impact on program synthesis. Their proposed method really has the potential to make these systems more accurate and efficient. With a bit more detail and some extra comparisons, this paper could be even better.

**Strengths:**
* Presents a truly novel approach to program synthesis, tackling two key limitations of current methods.
* Smartly uses reinforcement learning to focus on generating semantically correct programs.
* Introduces a valuable syntax checker to streamline the program generation process.
* Proposes an innovative joint learning method for when syntax rules aren't readily available.

**Weaknesses:**
* Needs more depth on the implementation details of the syntax checker and joint learning.
* Could benefit from more thorough comparisons, especially regarding computational efficiency and scalability.
* Should explore applying the approach to more complex programming languages and domains.

**Rating:** 8/10

**Recommendation:** Accept with minor revisions. This paper is a strong contribution to the field, and their method has real potential to improve program synthesis. Just a few more details and comparisons would make it even stronger.

This paper fits models to spike trains of retinal ganglion cells that are driven by natural images. I think the title should thus include the word “activity” at the end for otherwise it is actually formally incorrect.

Anyhow, this paper proposes more specifically a recurrent network for this time series prediction and compares it to what seems to be the previous approach of a generalized linear model. Overall the stated paradigm is that when one can predict the spikes well then one can look into the model and learn how nature does it. 

In general the paper sounds plausible, though I am not convinced that I learned a lot. The results in figure 2 show that the RNN model can predict the spikes a bit better. So this is nice. But now what? You have shown that a more complicated model can produce better fits to the data, though there are of course still some variations to the real data. Your initial outline was that a better predictive model helps you to better understand the neural processing in the retina. So tell us what you learned. I am not a specialist of the retina, but I know that there are several layers and recurrencies in the retina, so I am not so surprised that the new model is better than the GLM. 

It seems that more complicated recurrent models such as LSTM do not improve the performance according to a statement in the paper. However, comparisons on this level are also difficult as a more complex models needs more data. Hence, I would actually expect that more layers and even a more detailed model of the retina could eventually improve the prediction even further. 
I was also a bit puzzled that all the neurons in the network share all the same parameters (weights). While the results show that these simplified models can capture a lot of the spike train characteristics, couldn’t a model with free parameters eventually outperform this one (with correspondingly more training data)?

Summary: This paper applies multitask recurrent neural networks to the problem of predicting spiking responses of primate retinal ganglion cells to natural image stimuli. The authors fit two-layer RNNs with parameters shared across neurons and compare them against standard linear-nonlinear (LN) and generalized linear models (GLMs). They find that the RNNs consistently capture a larger fraction of explainable variance across both ON and OFF parasol cells in two separate experimental preparations. To understand the source of this improvement, the authors introduce a GLM-RNN hybrid model in which a linear spatial filter precedes recurrent temporal processing. This hybrid recovers a substantial portion of the performance gap, suggesting that richer temporal nonlinearities account for much of the RNN advantage, though spatial nonlinearities also contribute. The paper further demonstrates that the multitask framework yields more accurate and stable predictions than individually trained RNNs, and that good predictive performance can be achieved with surprisingly small amounts of training data.

Strengths: The paper tackles a timely and important problem at the interface of machine learning and computational neuroscience. The experimental analysis is rigorous and includes several well-designed controls, such as ablating receptive field patch size, comparing shared versus individual model training, and constructing the hybrid architecture to disentangle spatial and temporal contributions. The finding that multitask parameter sharing improves generalization in a data-limited neurophysiology setting is practically significant and well-supported by the results. The manuscript is clearly written, the methods are described in sufficient detail to permit reproduction, and the analysis of training data requirements addresses a key practical concern for applying deep learning to neural data. Overall, the study provides a convincing demonstration that flexible recurrent architectures can outperform classical models in sensory neuroscience.

Weaknesses: The network architectures explored are relatively standard, and the methodological novelty is limited primarily to the application domain rather than to learning algorithms or architectures. Despite the hybrid model, the internal computations of the full RNN remain largely uninterpreted, and the paper does not provide a detailed analysis of the specific temporal features or dynamics that the recurrent layers capture. The study is restricted to parasol ganglion cells from only two retinal preparations, which raises questions about how well the conclusions generalize to other retinal cell types, other species, or cortical circuits. The use of mean squared error on smoothed firing rates, rather than a point-process likelihood, is a questionable choice for modeling discrete spike trains, even though the authors note that Poisson likelihood optimization gave qualitatively similar results. Finally, the paper explicitly ignores correlations between neurons, which are known to carry substantial information in the retina; incorporating at least simple coupling terms could have strengthened the modeling framework.

Questions for the authors: How sensitive are the main conclusions to the choice of loss function, and would optimizing a Poisson or other point-process likelihood alter the relative ranking of the models or the interpretation of the hybrid results? Could you provide more concrete visualizations or examples of the temporal nonlinearities captured by the hybrid model that are absent in the GLM? Have you considered whether more biologically plausible constraints, such as localized connectivity or divisive normalization in the recurrent layers, would preserve performance while improving interpretability? How does model performance compare when trained on white noise versus natural scene stimuli, and does the RNN advantage persist across stimulus classes? Finally, what do you see as the main obstacle to extending this multitask RNN approach to larger, more heterogeneous neural populations or to cortical areas?

Recommendation: I recommend this paper for acceptance. While the architectures themselves are not novel, the work makes a solid empirical contribution by showing that multilayer recurrent networks and multitask learning can substantially improve predictive models of neural spiking responses. The careful experimental design, the practical insights for neuroscience, and the clear presentation make this a valuable paper for the ICLR audience. I would assign an overall score of 6, indicating a good paper that should be accepted, though not without the minor limitations noted above.

This paper explores whether nonlinear recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can account for neural response properties that have eluded other models. A multilayer RNN is trained to mimic the stimulus-response mapping observed in actual retinal ganglion cells responding to a sequence of natural images. The RNN performs significantly better than conventional LN/GLM models, particularly in capturing transient responses.

This work represents an important step toward understanding the nonlinear response properties of visual neurons. Recent results have shown that even the responses of retinal ganglion cells to natural movies are difficult to explain using standard receptive field models, presenting a significant challenge to the field. Even having *a* model that works would be a starting point, so this work should be viewed in that light. The challenge now, of course, is to determine what the RNN is actually doing. Perhaps it could be pruned and simplified to identify which components are critical to its performance; it would have been nice to see such an analysis. Nevertheless, this result is a promising first step and, in my view, important for the community to know about.

Review for ICLR 2017

Summary:
The paper proposes a method for neural network compression based on "soft weight-sharing," a technique originally introduced by Nowlan and Hinton in 1992. The authors frame the problem through the lens of the Minimum Description Length (MDL) principle, treating compression as a variational inference problem. Specifically, they model the weight prior as a mixture of Gaussians (GMM) and learn the mixture parameters (means, variances, and mixing proportions) simultaneously with the network weights using gradient descent. This approach allows the network to automatically determine the optimal number of clusters and the pruning rate (by fixing one component at zero). The final compression is achieved by quantizing weights to the nearest cluster mean and utilizing storage formats similar to those used by Han et al. (2015).

Strengths:
1. Theoretical Grounding: The paper provides a clear and principled connection between variational learning, the MDL principle, and model compression.
2. Unified Approach: The method integrates pruning and quantization into a single training procedure, rather than relying on the multi-step pipeline (pruning then quantizing) common in other state-of-the-art methods.
3. Flexibility: By learning the prior, the model can adaptively determine the necessary quantization intervals and the amount of pruning required per layer.
4. Strong Results on Small Models: The authors achieve state-of-the-art compression rates on MNIST-based models (LeNet) with negligible loss in accuracy.

Weaknesses:
1. Limited Scalability: The experimental results are primarily focused on small models. While a ResNet is mentioned, the authors admit that the algorithm is too slow for larger architectures like VGG. The proposed solution for scalability (sampling weights for the prior gradient) is discussed in the appendix but not experimentally validated.
2. Hyper-parameter Sensitivity: The authors note that the learning rates for the mixture components are "very sensitive" and that the mixture can collapse too quickly. The reliance on Bayesian optimization (Spearmint) to tune 13 different hyperparameters suggests that the method may be difficult to apply to new architectures without significant tuning effort.
3. Baseline Comparisons: While the results on LeNet are strong, the lack of comprehensive results on larger, modern datasets (like ImageNet) makes it difficult to assess if the method remains competitive against the highly optimized pipelines of Han et al. on complex tasks.
4. Implementation Complexity: The retraining process requires managing separate learning rates and potential hyper-priors (Inverse-Gamma, Beta) to prevent component collapse, which increases implementation complexity compared to simple post-training quantization.

Questions for the authors:
1. Regarding the scalability issue: You propose sampling K weights to approximate the prior gradient in Appendix C. Have you performed any preliminary tests to see if this maintains the same compression quality as the full gradient?
2. How does the total training time (including the Bayesian optimization phase) compare to the pipeline proposed by Han et al.?
3. You mentioned that the amount of pruning depends on the number of parameters in the layer. Do you have a theoretical explanation for why larger layers are more amenable to pruning in this framework?
4. Could you clarify the impact of the choice of the initial number of components (e.g., 17 for LeNet vs 64 for ResNet)? Is there a heuristic for choosing this number for an unknown architecture?

Recommendation:
Accept (Poster). The paper presents a mathematically sound and elegant way to unify pruning and quantization through the MDL principle. Although the experimental section is dominated by smaller models and the scalability to very large networks is not yet proven, the conceptual contribution is significant and provides a principled alternative to heuristic-based compression pipelines.

This paper proposes an empirical Bayesian approach to learn the parameters of a neural network and their corresponding priors. A mixture model prior over the weights leads to a clustering effect in the weight posterior distributions (which are approximated with delta peaks). This clustering effect can be exploited for the quantization and compression of network parameters. The authors demonstrate that this method achieves compression rates and predictive accuracies comparable to related approaches.

Earlier work [Han et al. 2015] is based on a three-stage process: pruning small-magnitude weights, clustering the remaining ones, and updating the cluster centers to optimize performance. The current work provides a more principled approach that avoids this ad-hoc multi-stage structure in favor of a single iterative optimization process.

The first experiment, described in Section 6.1, shows that an empirical Bayes approach—even without hyper-priors—already leads to a pronounced clustering effect and sets many weights to zero. In particular, a compression rate of 64.2 is obtained on the LeNet300-100 model. Note that in Section 6.1, the text refers to "Figure C," which I assume should be "Figure 1."

Section 6.2 describes an experiment where hyper-priors are used, and the parameters of these distributions, as well as other hyper-parameters like learning rates, are optimized using Spearmint (Snoek et al., 2012). Figure 2 shows the performance of different points evaluated in the hyper-parameter space (each trained network represents an accuracy-compression rate point on the graph). The text claims that the best results lie on a line; this seems a somewhat interpretation given the limited data. Moreover, it would be useful to add a brief discussion on whether such a linear relationship would be expected. Currently, the results of this experiment lack sufficient interpretation.

Section 6.3 presents results for CNN models and compares them to recent findings by Han et al. (2015) and Guo et al. (2016). Comparable results are obtained in terms of compression rate and accuracy. The authors state that their current algorithm is too slow to be useful for larger models such as VGG-19, though they briefly report some results for this model (without comparing them to related work). It would be helpful to explain what slows down the training compared to standard training without weight clustering, and how the proposed algorithm scales with respect to data volume and model size.

The contribution of this paper is largely experimental, leveraging standard ideas from empirical Bayesian learning to introduce weight clustering effects into CNN training. That said, it is an interesting result that such a relatively straightforward approach leads to results on par with state-of-the-art, yet more ad-hoc, network compression techniques. The paper could be improved by clearly describing the training algorithm and how it scales to large networks and datasets. Another point deserving further discussion is how the hyper-parameter search is performed (I assume test data is not used) and how the compared methods handled the search over hyper-parameters to determine the accuracy-compression tradeoff. Ideally, methods should be evaluated across multiple points on this trade-off curve.
